newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds whipped by inflation fears.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds whipped by inflation fears.

text.p: The stock market tumbled Thursday before ending the first session of 1997 just slightly weaker, but bonds failed to recover from an extended sell-off sparked by upbeat economic news that revived inflation fears.
Stocks scored modest gains as trading got underway, reassuring some investors after the Dow Jones industrial average fell 101 points on Tuesday, the last session of 1996.
But the market promptly headed south after a report of robust manufacturing activity in December sparked a steep decline in the bond market, which in turn hurt stocks.

The Dow industrials quickly fell 96 points, but stocks then wound their way higher during the rest of the session. Stocks got a final boost from computer-driven buy programmes in the final minutes. The 30-share Dow closed with a loss of 5.78 points at 6,442.49.
On the New York Stock Exchange, 1,848 stocks fell and 786 rose on active volume of 461 million shares.
Analysts said the heavy early selling appeared to be an over-reaction made possible in part because so many traders and investor were still enjoying New Year's vacations.

"I thought it would take until next week for the market to rebound but I have a feeling a lot of people that weren't working decided to call in late and say, 'Start buying these things'," said Robert Froehlich, chief investment strategist at Van Kampen American Capital.

According to Birinyi Associates, which tracks programme trading, the late buy programme reversed 51 points in Dow losses in a mere 10 minutes and sharply cut the losses in the Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks, which closed down 3.73 points at 737.01 after falling more than 11 points earlier.

The report that sparked the sell-off came from the National Association of Purchasing Management, which said its index of maufacturing activity rose to 54.0 in December, the highest in six months, from 52.7 in November. A reading above 50 points to growth in manufacturing, while one below that level indicates contraction.

The report signalled an economic pickup that could mean accelerating inflation and force the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates to control growth. The Fed has held rates steady since last January, when it cut rates to spur growth.
The report was the first major indicator of the new year and had been widely awaited in financial markets. Private economists had expected a reading of 51.5 for December.

Bonds skidded after the report. The 30-year Treasury bond fell 1-6/32 points, or $11.875 on a $1,000 bond, raising its yield to 6.74 percent -- the highest level since Oct. 28 -- from 6.64 percent on Tuesday. Bond prices and yields move in the opposite direction.
"We just tested 6.75 percent but didn't finish over that and that helped," said Froehlich at Van Kampen American. Bond yields approaching 7 percent tend to start drawing funds away from stocks.

The steep drop in stocks on Tuesday followed reports of a strong rise in consumer confidence in December and the fastest growth in new home sales in November in 3-1/2 years. While Tuesday's drop was confined mostly to blue-chip issues, Thursday's decline moved into the broader market.

The dollar slid as low as 1.5380 German marks and 115.30 Japanese yen. In late New York trading, the dollar settled at 115.58 yen Thursday, down from 116.08 yen Tuesday. It climbed to 1.5430 marks from 1.5400 marks.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, March wheat rose 8 cents a bushel to close at $3.89-1/4 as talk circulated on the trading floor that Egypt, a big buyer of American wheat, would soon purchase up to 500,000 metric tons.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, February crude oil ended 23 cents lower at $25.69 a barrel after setting a life-of-contract high of $26.05 earlier, as traders took profits from the week's gains.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index of blue-chip shares lost 61.1 points, or 1.5 percent, to close at 4,057.4. The Tokyo stock market was closed for a national holiday.
